[h1]Comentario Analítico: "RPG Maker 2000" (RPGM2k)[/h1]

Tras RPG Maker 95 en 1997 (Cuyo estreno internacional jamás llegó), acabamos por tener a RPG Tsukuru 2000 como exclusivo en Japón. Fue éste el primero de toda la serie de software en alcanzar a popularizarse en todo el mundo gracias a las iteraciones traducidas e ilegales de un usuario Ruso bajo el alias de 'Don Miguel', y no fue hasta mediados del 2015 que acabamos por tener una versión internacional de manera oficial a manos de KADOKAWA y Gotcha Gotcha Games.

La versión oficial e internacional de RPG Maker 2k es hoy por hoy casi tan versatil como RPG Maker 2k3 pues acabó recibiendo varias actualizaciones con las que se adaptó a algunas de las nuevas funciones de su sucesor; aún así, no tiene una pantalla completa a modo de ventana sin bordes como 2k3, cuanto con menos comandos a la carta y continúa en falta de algunas configuraciones como la opción de saltar la pantalla de menú por defecto (Para así armar un menú custom como en 2k3).

Fue acá en donde se introdujo los Common Events, las variables (Como alternativa de mayor complejidad a los Switches) y el Conditional Branch, además de ser un software mucho más estable que RPG Maker 95 (Que se volvió famoso por ser propenso a crashear).

El principal motivo para comprar RPG Maker 2000 por encima de 2003 está en el combate; el de 2k3 es Active Time Battle (ATB) y el de 2k es estrictamente por turnos; y la visualización de éstos también es distinta, en RPG Maker 2003 vemos a todos los combatientes de perfil mientras que en RPG Maker 2000 vemos al combate en primera persona.

En mi caso lo compré para ver si puedo contactar con un proxy y subir un mapa mío a Yume 2kki, pero lo veo complicado jaja. Para cualquiera que quiera hacer su propio juego, lo más seguro es ir con RPG Maker 2003 (A no ser que no te guste su modalidad de combate y prefieras la de 2000).

[b]¿En conclusión?[/b] Un antes y un después, sin éste no hubiéramos tenido al mejor RPG Maker de todos (A mi parecer cuanto menos), véase el 2003.

This game is top-down excellency! Being one of the first RPG Maker games to ever surface the world, it does its job with pride! If you're ever interested in creating an RPG with an easy-to-use, user friendly engine, then this game is perfect for you. 
RPG Maker 2000 uses three different planes in this game that I like to refer to as terrain, scenery, and events. Terrain is your normal ground, things that the player will walk on. Scenery is something the player can see or sometimes feel. Events are triggers or commands that perform a certain action. An event can be a battle, dialogue, a shop, or anything else your mind desires! 
RPG Maker 2000 uses its own pre-made assets, but you can of course import your own, which I love! You can also import your own music and other assets to really make the game feel like your own!
Overall, it is a great game for people who want to mess around with making their first RPG, or for experienced developers looking to be successful in the RPG world.

I don't recommend this steam version for commercial game dev for a number of reasons, though the engine itself is objectively good (and I'll always have a soft spot for it). 

If you're looking for an engine for serious game development, and the game isn't some kind of visual-novel-rpg or a casual gaming experience, then this will be a frustrating engine to use. If your're just a hobby game-maker, then this is excellent for its price (and you'll find *lots* of rm2k assets/resources online for non-commercial use)

Yet, I still regret paying any amount for the steam version, as it has a broken project import system. Anyway:

Pros:
1. It's cheaper than the later versions and pretty solid basic-rpg-feature-wise
2. Truly user-friendly - in that it has several limitations in favour of being easy to pick up and use for basic game-making, which is still very impressive considering when this engine first came out
3. Nostalgia-factor
4. Good for someone less technically inclined
5. Subjectively cooler graphics
Cons: 
1. It's really old and not supported much now anyway (from the devs)
2. The steam version doesn't let you import old projects, even if they were made using the same steam version but on another system. Import looks broken, tbh. This is a deal-breaker in my view 
3. You can *still* get the 'map tree corrupted' error and the workaround is *still* as long and partial and depressing as before, from what I'm aware of
4. Tedious command setup flows for events, can be an immense pain even for someone who doesn't like 'scripting'

Despite the pros outnumbering the cons, I'd still only recommend it if price is a factor and/or if you are not interested in making games with any level of complexity in any kind of mechanics - that's too many hours you'll burn because the engine isn't made keeping a programmer in mind, and so "programming" any level of generic, reusable behaviour with all the basic limitations is not really feasible.

I'm not aware how many of the RM2K limitations exist in the later versions (like being unable to reference switches through variables, for example), but if the later versions don't allow for much programming flexibility compared to rm2k, then you may as well stick with rm2k or look at some other engines out there. If programming features are not something you're looking for anyway, then this is a good engine to start with.

---Original Review---
This is RPG Maker 2000 in a [i]nearly[/i] perfect form, with a glaring exception that forces me to run both the JP Value!+ Version and this EN Version:
[b] No Japanese language support [/b]
Which is a damn shame, because this is otherwise the perfect RM2k package for those of us boomers who prefer to go old school, even if only for the fact that the event editor has colored text to differentiate between commands.

One of the real shames of the older gen ツクール titles is that a lot of the best learning resources, such as yado.tk, are accessible only to those who understand Japanese. Operating under the theory that a rising tide lifts all boats, Japanese users of RPG Maker went out of their way to make many high-quality tutorials which serve not only to teach one how to use RPG Maker's built-in tools to a high level, but to teach why and how they work so that a learner can easily transition into coming up with their own solutions to new problems not covered by them.

This, in stark contrast to the English community where googling "how to do (thing)" may only yield partial explanations, or vague motions in the direction of how to do something with no true knowledge being passed along. This, I assume is part of a more knowledge-hogging culture where nobody wishes to share their "secrets" with others, for fear that others might make something high-quality themselves. This has somewhat bled over into modern iterations of RPG Maker where people are less inclined to learn and problem solve for themselves, preferring simply to stack plugins to try and make their game "unique," only to end up making something that is not unique in the slightest when everybody else has used the same plugins to achieve the same ends.

Learning how to use the tools in 2k can set a user up for success and independence down the line, even as they move up to more modern editions of RPG Maker. Indeed, someone who understands the limits of this older title will be very pleased when they find they can do such things as[i] Call Common Event[/i]s during battle in 2k3 and beyond, or use [i]Self-Switches[/i]. By then, they may have already worked out clever ways to deal with the limitations set forth by 2k that can still be applied to their problem solving later on. They may also be dismayed at certain new limitations set forth by newer RPG Makers, but that is neither here nor there.

Is it every bit as clunky as it's ever been? Oh yeah. You will still want to use an external text editor of some sort to write all your dialogue, then copy+paste them into dialogue boxes. You will still need to manually set the transparent color of assets you import that have a transparent color different than whatever RM2k is expecting it to be. Eventing with the built-in event editor can be a real pain due to lack of certain abilities which would be nice. But that's just RM2k.

My biggest gripe outside of the inability to work with JP text or cleanly open JP titles (not an issue the other way around, ironically) is that the localization falls flat in certain areas. Where the Japanese version of the game is clear and concise with the terminology used, certain poorly translated sections add a sense of ambiguity and force me to refer back to the original game just to confirm precisely what some things will do or how they operate.

[i]Control Variables: [XXXX: Variable Name] = (item) in Inventory
Control Variables: [XXXX: Variable Name] = (item) not in Inventory[/i]

Is a solid example of an incorrect translation which may cause players trouble who are not already familiar with these commands, which more specifically check for [i]Items in Possession[/i] and [i]Items Equipped[/i]. There are other instances where it is worse than this, such as setting the calling conditions for Common Events. The Japanese game has a setting which explicitly sets such events to be used [i]Only When Called[/i], whereas the EN localization simply grays out that section, providing you only with the other two options of Autorun and Parallel Process. (By default, a common event will only be called when you call it, but that is not made abundantly clear when it's not explicitly listed as an option.)

None of it is as bad as the Don Miguel translation of yore, which had such gems as [i]Enter Password[/i] being used in the place of [i]Key Input[/i], [i]Stop Parallel Events[/i] in place of [i]End Event Processing[/i], and others, but I suppose that was the price to pay for not knowing Japanese back then...

This game/tool is worth every penny of its asking price, and I almost feel bad having paid $2.50 for it on sale, but they still got me when I had to pay much more than that for my JP copy, so I feel a bit less guilty.

I've been using RM2k since about 2006 and I was 10 years old when I released my first game in the engine. It's that easy to learn to use it, but it doesn't mean the engine has its limitations when you try to make more complex games. After a thousand hours spent in this Steam version doing a remake of my very first game, I may be able to review it in detail and explain most, if not every feature present.

Importing custom content:
It has a simple content import/export tool that's easy to use, but it doesn't explain what the file requirements are, when you get an error. Images have to be saved in 8-bit color mode and it accepts MP3 music in this version, which is nice. Movies are just a wreck, whether you're trying to import an AVI or a weird MPEG type file, it's just not worth it, because it increases the project's size greatly and most devices won't play the movie in-game. You can even hide content from players using the '.xyz' format while importing image content.

The Database:
Very simple and easy to use. You can create your own main characters, skills, items, enemies, terrain for the maps, edit the basic battle, menu and stores vocabulary and change the game's default BGM and Sound Effects for various stuff. My only complaint is that you can put some mid-battle events, but you can't call premade "Common Events" in them, so it's not modular in that way, in a programming point of view.

Map creation and drawing:
You can create hundreds of maps and I didn't find a limit yet. Every map is a separate '.lmu' file, so it's good for when you have to send just a small fix to your playerbase, or something like that. You can also define finite areas whithin the map where players can battle different enemy groups, or define the entire map to have the same enemy groups, but you can't enable/disable the areas or change which enemy groups appear, using events.
You're presented 3 layers of map drawing: a lower, an upper and an event one. The former two use the terrain Chipset, while the latter uses Charsets for NPCs and you can use them for map drawing as well, like a third layer of terrain.

Map events and programming in general:
You don't need to learn any programming language to use RPG Maker. The engine uses its event-based logic to dictate what happen when a player talks to a NPC or walk to another map, etc. It's good to know boolean logic if you want to make more complex events, though.
Here is where RPG Maker 2000 shows its true limitations, unfortunately. Simple things like multiple math equations in a single line are not possible, even though you can achieve that with a bunch of "Change variable" commands. Condition branches with "OR"s are non existant, so you'll have to copy commands to achieve the same result. Loops doesn't have a condition to leave them, so you'll have to force a "Condition branch" and "Break Loop". 
There were situations where I felt like programming in Assembly because of the goto and labels. There are no object-orientation or pointers AT ALL (and that's my biggest complaint). When you set an event to move, there is no option for it to wait until its movement is completed before proceeding, so often you'll have situations where you set a "Wait for all movement" command and the event will freeze because there are other events moving in the map (like enemies with random movement or moving toward the player).

Conclusion:
It's a neat engine, great for people who don't know programming at all or programmers looking for a challenging development project. Keep in mind that the game will only have a resolution of 320x240 (and you can scale it up to 2x, so 640x480) and you can only run it on a Windows machine (and some others via emulator, look up EasyRPG Player).
It's a good software, but get it on a sale, because you'll probably won't use it as much as I did.
